newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - US set for new year bounce over Bunds.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US set for new year bounce over Bunds.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are set to make inroads against German Bunds early next year as growth continues on a steady path, interest rates stay on hold and concerns about financial market exuberance fade, analysts said on Tuesday.

The U.S. Federal Reserve's policy-setting arm was likely to keep rates level at its meeting later on Tuesday, despite recent warnings from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan about the economic damage that can be wrought by bursting financial bubbles.
The meeting should set the stage for spread narrowing between 10-year U.S. and German bonds, analysts said.
"We will start to see asset allocation decisions in the first quarter back into the U.S.," Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London said.
The T-note/Bund spread was quoted at 60 basis points at 1215 GMT, having moved in Germany's favour in recent days as U.S. yields shot up on Greenspan's comments.

Chester said the spread may bulge a little further Germany's way through Christmas but should edge back towards 40 basis points in the first quarter of 1997 as the dollar appreciates and good news on the U.S. budget filters through.

While Chester was waiting to see how the Christmas sales period pans out, he expected U.S. growth to stay on trend at around two percent in the first half of 1997. This should provide the main underpinning for Treasuries' outperformance.
Although the market was more nervous than usual about the the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, after Greenspan's comments earlier this month, the result should not be troubling.
The Fed could even move towards a neutral policy bias from the tightening bias of late summer and early autumn, they said.

"There is an outside chance that we'll get a small tightening but the odds are heavily against it," said George Magnus, chief international economist at UBS in London. "The real economic data just don't justify it."
Magnus said the data might even point to a slight easing in rate policy early next year before tightening later in the year.
He argues that consumption remains weak, consumer credit has dropped off considerably and capital expenditure has left the days of double digit growth behind.

"The consumer is going through a period of balance sheet surgery," Magnus said. "We've still got fairly buoyant trends in real income growth but the savings rate has been gradually built back up again in recent months and it may be this consumer pause will go on into the spring of 1997."
Magnus said the T-note/Bund spread will likely fluctuate between 50 and 70 basis points between now and the end of the year but it will take another stab at 25 in the first quarter.
He said that move would be helped by some liquidation of foreign holdings of Bunds in 1997, as impending currency union eventually takes the shine off mark assets.
Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London, said Bunds could come under pressure short-term as the market digests the Bundesbank's monthly report released earlier on Tuesday.

Echoing the drift of some of Greenspan's comments, the central bank report condemned efforts to boost growth through monetary easing during periods of low inflation, saying such moves risked creating uncertainty and market turbulence.
Analysts said the report clearly spelled out the chance of further German rate easing was slim.
"On balance the Bundesbank report was quite bearish for Bunds," Knuthsen said. Longer term though, inflation will remain low and Bund yields will only move gradually higher, he added.
"In the U.S. we are a bit more optimistic on growth and we still think the Fed will raise rates, so there is a clear economic basis for Bunds outperforming Treasuries," he said.
